Case A

A1. The search covered only the past seven days and returned only the earlier requests from the stable region and fingerprint. The 19-minute burst therefore looks like the first misuse within that window. But the key was published, and the search covers requests the key made, so earlier misuse before the window can't be excluded. The question asks whether the burst at 19 minutes was the first misuse. The seven-day search shows no other requests, which suggests it was the first. Still, the earlier requests could in principle include misuse from the same region, and the search scope is limited to the seven days. "Cannot tell" fits best, since the key may have been published earlier than the seven-day window, and the publication time relative to that window isn't given. The burst came 19 minutes after publication, and everything in the seven days before it was one stable pattern, so no misuse is evident before the burst. Even so, the earlier requests were consistent with the owner, and the stable pattern is not shown to be benign. I choose Cannot tell.

A2. The check scored the account 30 minutes after publication, when the burst was already visible. The burst included a new fingerprint, a proxy, a payout change and a faster schedule. Whether the check had access to those signals isn't stated. Cannot tell.

A3. A shared payout destination does not by itself show a single owner. No, not by itself.

A4. After 30 days, no report or finding was recorded. Absence of reports is weak evidence at best, since nobody may have looked. Of the listed options, "Yes, weakly" and "No" are both defensible. The payouts went to a destination shared with two other accounts, and no review is recorded. Absence of a recorded finding is not evidence of legitimacy when nobody is shown to have looked. I choose Cannot tell.

A5. Yes. The burst involved a changed payout destination, a new fingerprint through a proxy, and a faster schedule, soon after publication.

Case B

B1. D has 0 chargebacks on 100 transactions against 2 for each of the others, so its rate is lower. Yes.

B2. A combined 5 percent doesn't show that no single account is above 5 percent. Chargebacks alone are 6 of 400, or 1.5 percent, so the 5 percent measure includes alerts, which are not broken down by account. Cannot tell.

B3. The search found no accounts beyond A and the closed account, but it only covers the searched identifiers. It doesn't show there are none under other identities. No.

B4. Two notes by different analysts on different days may still rest on the same evidence. Independence isn't shown. Cannot tell.

B5. A blocked payment with no chargeback isn't shown to be non-fraud, because blocking prevents the chargeback. No.

B6. Shared templates, descriptor pattern and a link through A justify investigating together. Yes.

RESULT MN-079 | A1: Cannot tell | A2: Cannot tell | A3: No, not by itself | A4: Cannot tell | A5: Yes | B1: Yes | B2: Cannot tell | B3: No | B4: Cannot tell | B5: No | B6: Yes
